Location: Bidur, Nepal

Disaster: Floods, 2026

Isha Rimal is a 17-year-old volunteer for the Red Cross Society in Bidur, Nepal. This summer, her family was caught up in the floods that crashed through the country after a glacier collapsed – an event made more likely by climate change

From the roof of our home we can see the Himalayan goddesses. That is what the mountains mean to us: they are goddesses. I grew up here in Bidur, Nuwakot, two hours from Kathmandu. It is a beautiful place with a perfect climate. Or so I used to think, before the Bhotekoshi flood waters from the glacier collapse tore down the Trishuli River, destroyed many homes and killed some of my friends.

View image in fullscreen Isha has volunteered with the Red Cross Society since the disaster.

It changed my life. Until then I had planned to study in the US and become a neuroscientist. But now I want to stay here, train as a medical doctor and help my people.

I thought it was an earthquake at first. The house was shaking. My bed was shaking.

I was alone at home. My younger brother and sister were at school, but I was sleeping in because I’d just graduated. At about 9am I got a call from my mum. She told me to come as fast as I could to the college where she worked. She didn’t say why, but she sounded worried. So I got out of bed, locked the house and left as fast as I could. I only had 10% power on my phone.

View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the flood. Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

It is a 10-minute walk from my home to the college. My mum had told me to hurry, so I ran. Everyone was in a hurry and running. Many were going down towards the river – the opposite direction from me. I remember a strange smell.

I didn’t talk to anyone, so I didn’t know what was happening. All that was going through my head was trying to guess why mum had called me. She had never done that before, not while she was at work.

I never imagined the threat could come from the river. That’s also 10 minutes’ walk from my home. My friends and I used to go there as children. People would bathe there. We live among rivers. They had never been something to be scared of.

When I reached the college, I found my mum. She had been informed about the flood. We never imagined it could be so big. Everybody was chattering; there were rumours that all the buildings had collapsed. Mum started crying. She said my brother and sister’s school had been affected, and she hadn’t been able to reach them.

It is difficult for me to remember all my frightened feelings at that time. We didn’t know if we were safe. We learned the bridge had been washed away, so there was no way to go to the other side. There were rumours of more floods. And my brother and sister were missing.

We had no way of knowing where they had gone. Police had turned up at their school in Bidur and told the students to flee. Teachers packed as many as they could in the school bus, but there was only one bus and hundreds of students. The others were just told to run as fast as they could. We asked a relative to look for them on a motorbike. He found my sister. But my brother took more time. He had hitched a lift with some foreigners and reached very high ground. We were crying with worry, and it turned out he had been eating ice-cream!

View image in fullscreen A debris-strewn residential street after the devastating flash floods in Devighat, Nuwakot. Photograph: Sunil Pradhan/Anadolu/Getty Images

When the river calmed, we went home. But everything was chaotic. The flood had knocked out two hydropower plants. The phone signals in many areas were down, and there was no electricity. The fans and air conditioning didn’t work, so it was too hot to sleep at night. There was also so much noise from the rescue helicopters.

It has been traumatic. Many died. One of my childhood friends was killed. Others lost their homes. After a while, the bodies of dead people and animals started to smell. Many people are psychologically affected by what happened, by seeing the collapsed homes. My brother and sister were so scared that we sent them to Kathmandu for four days.

Two days later, we had another flood. I don’t think anyone reported it. From then on, there were constant rumours about other floods. And fake alerts, even at 2am. These made people evacuate, and some homes were robbed.

View image in fullscreen Houses partly submerged in muddy water along the riverside at Trishuli Bazar in Nuwakot. Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty Images

I didn’t dare visit the disaster area for many weeks. When I finally got the courage, I was shocked to see that places in Devighat I used to visit were gone. A temple where I had worshipped, gardens where our family had spent happy times together, markets where we used to shop, all gone. All those memories, gone.

I volunteered for the Red Cross. At first I worked for 30 days in the pharmacy of the emergency clinic. With the local bridge broken, many community members were left stranded and unable to reach Trishuli hospital for urgent care. As a volunteer, I’ve been on the ground assisting our pharmacists with medical inventory, listing treatments and dispensing free medicine directly to those in need.

Seeing people leave our clinic relieved, happy and deeply grateful to the Red Cross for providing what they needed most during this disaster has been the most rewarding experience.

After that, I trained with the sanitation team and learned how to advise people to wash their hands and use water purification tablets. This was important, because many water sources were contaminated.

In some areas the need is still very great. There were many NGOs here immediately after the flood, but most of them have gone. I guess there was no way for them to leave enough for everyone for a lifetime. But many didn’t even provide for five months.

I will continue volunteering until the end of December, then I will go to Kathmandu to study for my entrance exam for medical school.

My thinking has changed. I used to think that life was sorted, and now I have seen how quickly people can be affected. I used to want to be a neuroscientist and have fun in New York, but after seeing the doctors in the clinic I want to help people like they do. I love that. Now I feel happy to stay here and distribute medical treatment. It makes me feel happy when people thank me for doing that. I realise now that I don’t want to leave my country. I want to be here. I want to be a good doctor.

But we must change things. I still love mountains, but now I think people must be more respectful of mountains. We should not treat the climate as a big joke. We shouldn’t mess with it. The Bhotekoshi flood proved that climate change does not respect borders. While our nation contributes almost nothing to global emissions, our people are left rebuilding their lives inside cracked and damaged walls. I think other countries should take more responsibility, but we cannot be negligent here. This is a sign. We need to take the climate as a serious issue. Everyone around the world should do what they can. I am not asking for donations for Nepal; I am asking that everyone minimise the way they are affecting us. If we continue to ignore the melting Himalayas today, the consequences will flow down to everyone’s doorstep tomorrow.

full_article:
An environmental group from Nepal has appealed for cross-border cooperation on disasters at COP31, the UN climate change conference, in Turkey. An area along the Nepal-China border was devastated by mudslides in August.

The group of mostly young climate activists hosted an event at the COP31 venue on Wednesday.

The group's leader, Dikshya Subedi, spoke about the mudslide disaster. Her relatives are among the survivors. Subedi said the disaster highlighted problems with climate justice. She said this discussion is very important because countries and communities that have contributed the very least to climate change are facing similar disasters every year.

People from Nepal's neighbors, such as India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, attended the event. They discussed ways to procure funds to cover losses from climate-linked disasters and compensation, and to establish a system for data-sharing and early warnings. The participants confirmed the need for countries affected by climate change to step up cooperation.

A woman from Bhutan said it's good that the people of Nepal want to take action. She expressed hope they can unite, put up a stronger front and demand climate justice and climate finance in a fair form.

Subedi also said regional cooperation is necessary because climate change has no borders. She said this time it was Nepal, but the next time it could be another country. She called for urgent preparations, saying the climate crisis is already here and there is no time left.

Kathmandu, Nov 12: Minister for Information and Communications, Dr Bikram Timilsina, has held a discussion with Estonian Minister for Justice and Digital Affairs, Liisa-Ly Pakosta, on expansion of bilateral cooperation in the fields of digital transformation and e-governance.

During the meeting held in Doha, Qatar in course of the participation in the International Telecommunication Union (ITU)'s 'World Telecommunication Policy Forum 2026', the two ministers discussed the possibility of cooperation in the fronts of digital public infrastructure, e-governance system, digital transformation, cyber security and institutional capacity building.

Minister Dr Timilsina hailed the achievements Estonia made in the field of digital governance and expected that Nepal could gain important experience and learning from it. "The system developed by Estonia to make public service delivery technology-friendly, effective, transparent and citizen-centric could be useful for Nepal," he added.

Estonia is a pioneering country in successfully practicing digital governance. It has developed digital identity, secure data exchange, electronic signatures and online public service systems.

According to the Minister, the developing and underdeveloped countries should be benefitted from the knowledge, experience and resources gained by the developed countries in digital technology. The leading countries like Estonia can play a more active role in reducing the digital divide through the International Telecommunication Union, he viewed.

On the occasion, Estonian Minister Pakosta pledged advancing mutual cooperation and partnership with Nepal in the fields of digital transformation and e-governance. The experience and knowledge gained by Estonia in the course of developing the digital governance system can be shared with Nepal, she informed, adding that there is adequate potential for cooperation between the two countries in areas of mutual interest.

If cooperation between Nepal and Estonia in the digital transformation can be expanded, it can contribute to increasing the effectiveness of public service delivery, transparency in government processes, saving administrative costs and time and expanding access to services for citizens, according to her.

It is believed that Estonia's experience can be useful in Nepal's efforts to mainstream digital services in rural areas, remote communities and the citizens with limited access to digital infrastructure and technology. It can be ensured by expanding access to digital infrastructure and technology.

Even the good governance, citizen trust, data security and inclusive development can be matte of cooperation, it was stressed. (RSS)

title: Foreign Minister Khanal urges to keep mountain agenda at center of global climate action - The Rising Nepal
description: Foreign Minister Khanal urges to keep mountain agenda at center of global climate action  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Antalya (Turkiye), Nov 12: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has said that the effects of growing climate crisis are not being limited to mountain regions alone but affect the global economy, ecological systems, and human life, and therefore, mountain resilience should be placed at the center of global climate action.

Speaking at a discussion held today here under the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP-31) on the topic 'Advancing the Mountain Agenda: Melting Temperatures, Shared Responsibility, and Sustainable Financing for Glaciers, Snowfields, and Resilience,' he noted that the melting of glaciers, shrinking snowfields, and increasing disaster risks in mountain regions are adding challenges to global water and food security.

'When the mountains are in crisis, all of humanity is in trouble,' he said. 'Our glaciers and mountain peaks, which have formed over thousands of years, are changing rapidly within human lifetimes. The impact reaches not only mountains but also river systems, economies, ecosystems, and eventually the seas.'

Minister Khanal pointed out that climate change risks for Nepal are not just theoretical issues but a reality linked to direct human and physical damage, presenting the devastating flood in Nepal's Himalayan region on August 26 as an example.

Referring to the event as a 'Himalayan tsunami,' he explained that the fast-flowing sediment-laden flood caused by the collapse of glaciers and rocks had a serious impact on human lives, bridges, hydropower structures, and the livelihoods of local communities.

He noted that countries like Nepal, which contribute negligibly to global greenhouse gas emissions, bear a disproportionate burden of the climate crisis.

Emphasizing the need to accelerate global emission reductions to achieve the target of limiting temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius, he stated even if temperatures temporarily rise and then fall again, the glaciers that melted and the destroyed communities will not immediately return to their previous state. 'For mountainous nations, exceeding the temperature limit is not just a temporary statistical deviation; its consequences are long-term,' he added.

Minister Khanal presented five priorities on behalf of Nepal for the protection of mountainous areas and enhancing climate resilience.

These priorities include ambitious emission reduction, grant-based climate finance, effective loss and damage management, science-based monitoring and early warning systems, and institutional recognition of mountain issues within the United Nations climate change framework.

He emphasized that predictable, easily accessible, and grant-based climate finance should be provided to mountain countries for adaptation, resilient infrastructure, and sustainable livelihoods.

He believed that it is not fair to force disaster-affected and at-risk countries to rebuild solely through loans.

Similarly, he argued resources from the loss and damage fund should be delivered quickly, directly, and fairly to frontline mountain communities.

He also called for increased investment in regular glacier monitoring, satellite-based observation, regional data exchange, and multi-hazard early warning systems.

He also shared that Nepal has proposed the ‘From the Himalaya to the Sea’ partnership to promote collaboration, knowledge exchange, and collective efforts between mountain and coastal communities.

Highlighting that Nepal’s ‘Sagarmatha Call for Action’ has provided a clear roadmap for implementing the mountain agenda, he stressed that international cooperation is necessary to make the proposed UN Decade of Mountain Resilience effective.

The programme saw participation from Minister for Agriculture, Forests and Environment Gita Chaudhary, MPs and senior government officials from Nepal, as well as ministers and representatives from countries including Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Bhutan, and Pakistan. (RSS)

The U.S. Embassy in Nepal is urging the public to report suspected visa fraud, saying the State Department is stepping up efforts to detect and prevent attempts to enter the United States through fraudulent means or for unlawful purposes.

In a post on X, the embassy directed people to travel.state.gov/reportvisafraud, where they can submit information about suspected visa fraud.

“The Department of State is conducting rigorous fraud detection and prevention activities to thwart attempts to travel to the United States through fraudulent means or for illegal purposes,” the embassy said.

A Nepali-language graphic accompanying the post described a U.S. visa as a privilege, not a right, and encouraged the public to help authorities by reporting suspected fraud.

The State Department’s reporting page allows members of the public to submit information about potential visa fraud or misuse anonymously. Those who provide their names and email addresses may be contacted for additional information.

The department encourages people to provide as many details as possible, saying identifying information can increase the likelihood that a report will lead to a successful investigation. Information submitted through the form may be used to initiate or support law enforcement investigations or reviews of immigration actions, according to the department’s privacy notice.

The appeal comes as Nepali nationals face additional requirements when applying for certain U.S. visas. Nepal is among the countries subject to the U.S. visa bond requirement for B-1/B-2 visitor visas, which cover temporary travel for business or tourism. The requirement took effect for Nepali nationals on Jan. 21, 2026.

Under the policy, applicants traveling on Nepali passports who are otherwise eligible for B-1/B-2 visas must post a bond of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000. A consular officer determines the amount during the visa interview. The requirement applies regardless of the country in which the applicant submits the application.

The State Department instructs applicants to make payments only after receiving directions from a consular officer and to use the government’s designated payment process. Posting a bond does not guarantee that a visa will be issued.

title: Wild Elephants Cause Fear in Nepal Border Villages - Ratopati
description: Wild Elephants Cause Fear in Nepal Border Villages  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Jhapa. Fear has spread in the villages on the Nepal side after 14 wild elephants took shelter in the no-man's land area of Mechinagar Municipality-7 today all day. The no-man's land area where the elephants took shelter has bushes of sissoo and teak saplings growing in the Indian territory to the east. On the Nepal side, there are dense human settlements like Satighatta, Mechibasti, and Gairigaon.

Eyewitness GR Dhital said that a herd of elephants, including small calves, was seen in the bushes near the no-man's land since this morning. He said, "Those elephants have been staying there all day. We are afraid they might enter the village at any time."

To prevent the elephants from entering the settlements on the Nepal side, the Armed Police Force No. 2 Battalion, various BOPs, and security personnel deployed from the Division Forest Office Jhapa have increased security deployment at the border, said Ram Bhagat Yadav, acting chief of the Division Forest Office Jhapa.

Although the elephants coming from India have been stopped at the border, the local residents are afraid that the herd might enter the village at night. The members of 18 families in the Indian settlement east of the bushes where the elephants took shelter have left their homes since morning. Some of the residents of the Indian settlement who left their homes to save their lives are taking shelter in houses on the Nepal side, while some have gone to India via a roundabout route in Nepal.

The District Administration Office Jhapa had stated that security personnel have been deployed in the border area since Wednesday to stop the herd of elephants trying to enter Nepal from Prasad Gauda of Mechinagar-4.

The herd of elephants, which could not enter Nepal from the Bahunḍaṅgā border area of Mechinagar-4, changed its route and has been relocated to Mechinagar-7 from under the Mechi bridge about five kilometers south.

Chief District Officer Shravan Kumar Pokharel informed that security has been heightened on the Indian side to send the elephants back to India after elephants entered Nepal from Indian territory, destroying local residents' houses and eating ripe paddy.

To completely prevent the entry of elephants and to avoid potential damage, the Armed Police Force, Nepal Police, forest rangers from the Division Forest Office, Rapid Response Team, various organizations, and local farmers have been actively involved.
